triggers: a kernel on AMD MI308X (CDNA3 / gfx942) risks the '8. All Barriers in a 1-wave Kernel Are Redundant — Removing Them Gains +5-7%' trap

payload.goal: Avoid a known trap on AMD MI308X (CDNA3 / gfx942): 8. All Barriers in a 1-wave Kernel Are Redundant — Removing Them Gains +5-7%

problem.statement: Pitfalls: FlyDSL Attention Backward dQ + dK+dV on MI308X (gfx942) -- 8. All Barriers in a 1-wave Kernel Are Redundant — Removing Them Gains +5-7%

payload.attempted: The backward kernel has multiple `__syncthreads()` barriers protecting LDS write-after-read (WAR) and read-after-write (RAW) dependencies (P^T write → P^T read, cooperative load → LDS read, dS write → dS read). These barriers are required under multi-wave execution.
payload.lesson: For a 1-wave kernel (BLOCK_SIZE ≤ 64), all LDS barriers are redundant. You can safely remove them, but always verify correctness first. The forward kernel uses BLOCK_SIZE=256 (4 waves), so barriers must be retained there.

established_fact.mechanism: BLOCK_SIZE=64 = 1 wavefront = 64 lanes. Within the same wavefront, LDS writes are automatically visible to subsequent LDS reads (no out-of-order execution within a wavefront; VALU/LDS instructions complete in program order). Barriers only matter for synchronization between multiple wavefronts. Under 1-wave, `__syncthreads()` becomes pure overhead (~20 cycles stall per barrier).

payload.observed: Removing all barriers under 1-wave (BLOCK_SIZE=64): dQ +3.0%, dK+dV +5.4%.
